subject: religious-studies
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: A common misconception about prejudice is that:
options: Only certain groups can ever hold prejudiced attitudes
Anyone, from any background, can hold prejudiced attitudes
Prejudice is an unfair pre-judgement
Prejudice can be challenged through education
questions.explain: Prejudice is not limited to any one group; people of any background can hold prejudiced views.

questions.q: What does the 'parable of the Sheep and the Goats' teach about social justice?
options: The poor should be ignored
People will be judged by how they treated the hungry, sick and imprisoned
Wealth is the only measure of a good life
Charity is forbidden
questions.explain: In this parable, Jesus teaches that caring for the needy is like serving God himself, supporting social justice.

questions.q: What is 'social justice'?
options: Ignoring inequality
Removing all laws
Working towards a fair society where everyone has equal opportunities and rights
Giving advantages only to the rich
questions.explain: Social justice seeks fairness in society, including equal rights and opportunities for all.

questions.q: What is meant by the 'responsibilities of wealth'?
options: That the wealthy owe nothing to anyone
That money cannot help others
That those with money have a duty to use it to help others
That wealth must always be hidden
questions.explain: Many traditions teach that wealth carries a moral responsibility to support those in need.

questions.q: What is 'racism'?
options: Support for human rights
Prejudice or discrimination based on a person's race or ethnicity
A form of religious charity
Treating all races equally
questions.explain: Racism is prejudice or discrimination against people because of their race or ethnic background.

questions.q: What is 'positive discrimination'?
options: Ignoring all forms of inequality
Treating everyone exactly the same in every situation
Favouring members of a disadvantaged group to help correct past inequality
Refusing to employ anyone
questions.explain: Positive discrimination means giving an advantage to a disadvantaged group to address past unfairness, which is itself debated.

questions.q: Which religious teaching is often used to support equality?
options: That all people are made in the image of God and are of equal worth
That only some people matter to God
That discrimination is encouraged
That wealth determines worth
questions.explain: The belief that all are created in God's image is widely used to support human equality.

questions.q: Which figure is famous for campaigning against racial discrimination using non-violent methods and inspiring many believers?
options: William Paley
Charles Darwin
Richard Dawkins
Martin Luther King Jr
questions.explain: Martin Luther King Jr, a Christian minister, led the non-violent civil rights movement against racial discrimination.

questions.q: Which is an example of 'exploitation of the poor'?
options: Giving to charity
Offering fair pay
Paying unfairly low wages or charging unjust high interest
Providing free education
questions.explain: Exploitation includes unfair wages, excessive interest and taking advantage of vulnerable people.

questions.q: What is 'Fairtrade'?
options: A ban on international trade
A way of avoiding paying workers
A scheme ensuring producers in poorer countries receive a fair price for their goods
A type of luxury tax
questions.explain: Fairtrade aims to give producers in developing countries a fair price, addressing the exploitation of the poor.

questions.q: What is the difference between prejudice and discrimination?
options: Prejudice is an attitude; discrimination is acting on that attitude
Discrimination is always positive
Prejudice always involves action
They are exactly the same
questions.explain: Prejudice is an unfair attitude, while discrimination is unfair treatment based on it.

questions.q: Which is often cited as a cause of poverty?
options: Too much charity
Strong social justice
Unfair trade, conflict and lack of education or opportunity
Excessive equality
questions.explain: Causes of poverty include unfair trade, conflict, exploitation and lack of access to education.

questions.q: What are 'human rights'?
options: Basic freedoms and protections that belong to all people
Rules that apply to one country only
Privileges only for the wealthy
Rights given only by religion
questions.explain: Human rights are fundamental entitlements believed to belong to every person.

questions.q: Which is an example of 'religious discrimination'?
options: Refusing someone a job because of the faith they follow
Allowing people to worship freely
Providing prayer rooms for everyone
Treating all religions equally
questions.explain: Religious discrimination is treating someone unfairly because of their religion or beliefs.

questions.q: Which describes a non-religious basis for supporting human rights?
options: A claim that rights are unimportant
A rejection of all equality
A belief that rights come only from God
A belief in shared human dignity and reason rather than divine command
questions.explain: Humanists and others base human rights on shared human dignity, empathy and reason.

questions.q: Which describes a religious reason for opposing all forms of prejudice?
options: Belief requires excluding outsiders
Faiths teach that only some people matter
Many faiths teach that every person is equally valued and loved by God
Religion encourages judging by appearance
questions.explain: Many religions teach that all people have equal worth before God, which is used to oppose prejudice and discrimination.

questions.q: Why do many Christians give to charity, following the teaching of the 'Good Samaritan'?
options: Because they should help only their own family
Because they should help anyone in need, regardless of who they are
Because charity earns instant wealth
Because only the rich deserve help
questions.explain: The parable of the Good Samaritan teaches believers to help anyone in need, even strangers or enemies.

questions.q: What does 'religious freedom' mean?
options: The right of one religion to dominate all others
The right to hold and practise (or not practise) a religion of one's choice
Forcing everyone to share one belief
A ban on all religion
questions.explain: Religious freedom is the right to follow, change or reject a religion without persecution.

questions.q: What is 'prejudice'?
options: Judging someone unfairly before knowing them
Acting on good evidence
A type of charity
Treating everyone equally
questions.explain: Prejudice is a pre-formed, usually negative, opinion about someone not based on reason or experience.

questions.q: What do many religions teach about wealth?
options: The poor should be ignored
Wealth is always evil
Wealth is acceptable if used responsibly and shared with those in need
Charity is forbidden
questions.explain: Many faiths teach that wealth itself is not wrong, but it brings a duty to help others.

questions.q: Why do many faiths encourage charity (e.g. zakat, tithing, almsgiving)?
options: Because the poor do not deserve help
Because charity has no spiritual value
Because wealth should never be shared
Because helping the poor is seen as a religious duty
questions.explain: Practices like zakat and tithing show that caring for the poor is widely viewed as a duty.

questions.q: What does 'absolute poverty' mean?
options: Lacking the basic essentials needed to survive, such as food, clean water and shelter
Choosing to live simply for religious reasons
Having slightly less money than one's neighbours
Owning fewer luxuries than the rich
questions.explain: Absolute poverty means lacking the basic necessities for survival, unlike relative poverty which compares people within a society.
